items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals , have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish , levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time. Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data PFOS and PFOA PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals. PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer . The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. Results from the latest Environment Agency figures The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said. Lower concentrations, same total load Where forever chemicals go after a ban The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating. Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job. Making polluters pay Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said. Regulating PFAS as a group 15,000 compounds, 200 in common use PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment. Wider monitoring The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It’s 6 p.m. on a Friday, and the dinner you booked two weeks ago is in an hour. Back then it sounded like the perfect plan. But now your couch has never looked softer, your sweatpants feel like a hug, and your thumb is hovering over a message that starts with “So sorry, something came up…” Nothing came up, of course. You just don’t want to go anymore, and you can’t quite explain why. If that sounds familiar, you have plenty of company. According to the Survey Center on American Life , 55 percent of Gen Z adults say they feel relief when plans fall through. In the U.K., research from the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that 68 percent of people under 34 have bailed on plans, and one in 10 do it “very often.” There’s a name for that late-afternoon dread, and once you can name it, it gets a lot easier to put your shoes on anyway. What anticipatory anxiety feels like The doorway as a dividing line Mindy DeSeta , a licensed mental health counselor, calls it anticipatory anxiety. “It’s the stress we feel before something happens,” she says. Part of the pull comes from home itself, which is familiar and predictable in a way a crowded restaurant isn’t. “Walking through the doorway is the visual trigger that separates your safe space from the unknown,” DeSeta said. It’s the same jittery feeling you might have had before a school recital or a big presentation at work, just pointed at something that’s supposed to be fun. Why the dread rarely matches the night Think back to the last time you went out despite wanting to cancel. Chances are, an hour in, you were laughing at something and had forgotten all about the couch. DeSeta has seen that pattern again and again. “In most cases, the anticipation anxiety is often worse than the event itself. Don’t allow the jitters to deter you!” she said. What canceling plans costs your friends When everyone bails, everyone feels it Canceling feels harmless in the moment, and sometimes it’s the right call. But when it becomes a habit for a whole generation, someone is always on the other end of that text. Rachel Schleider, a 23-year-old social strategist said her birthday has become a source of stress for exactly this reason. “I literally dread making plans for my birthday every year because I know people are going to cancel the day before,” she said. She thinks the culture around flaking has swung too far. “We’ve kind of taken it too far and now people are way too comfortable bowing out,” Schleider said. How to manage anticipatory anxiety before a plan Name it, then don’t negotiate with it DeSeta’s first suggestion is to call the feeling what it is. Once you recognize the dread as anticipatory anxiety, you can remind yourself that the feeling isn’t an instruction. Feeling uneasy about going is a different thing from having a reason not to go. Breathe, and look at what the nerves are telling you A few slow, deep breaths can take the edge off the physical side of it, the tight chest and the restless hands. It also helps to flip the meaning of the nerves around. Feeling jittery about seeing someone usually means the plan matters to you, which is a reason to show up instead of a reason to stay home. Set an alarm and let the routine carry you DeSeta’s most practical trick happens before the dread has a chance to build: set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, get in the shower and get dressed without debating it. By the time your hair is dry, you’re most of the way out the door. None of this means you should drag yourself out when you’re sick or running on empty. Rest is a valid reason to cancel. But if the only thing standing between you and your friends is that familiar pre-plan heaviness, it might help to picture the walk home afterward, a little tired and full and glad you went, and let that version of the evening make the decision for you. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Although vegans generally have a healthy gut microbiome, they may be at risk of having lower gut bacterial diversity than omnivores, according to the author of a new study. The gut is home to billions of microorganisms. It is a complex ecosystem that regulates many of the body’s functions and helps keep us healthy—when it is in balance. Our diet influences this ecosystem. But what role does it play whether a person is vegan or omnivorous? In a new study, researchers from the University of Copenhagen examined this question by closely investigating the gut microbiome of 75 vegans and 75 omnivorous Danes. The researchers initially expected the vegan group to have the healthiest gut microbiome across all parameters. However, they found one notable weakness: gut bacterial diversity was, on average, lower among vegans than among omnivores. “This came as a major surprise. Because vegans eat only plant-based foods and therefore consume large amounts of dietary fiber and other health-promoting plant compounds that stimulate the gut microbiome, we expected the vegan group to have greater bacterial diversity than the omnivores. But that was not the case,” says Oluf Borbye Pedersen, professor at the Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research. He adds: “The study suggests that the lower average diversity of gut bacteria among vegans may be linked to their lower protein intake. Among vegans, 12% of dietary energy came from protein, compared with 17% among omnivores. However, the vegans who consumed the most protein had biodiversity levels comparable to those of the omnivores. Protein may therefore be an overlooked factor for a diverse gut microbiome among vegans.” The researchers are interested in gut health because it is crucial to overall health. In this context, having a diversity of bacteria is considered beneficial. “Our gut is an enormously complex ecosystem. It can be compared to a rainforest, which functions best when it houses as many different species as possible. The same applies to our internal microbial ecosystem. It should ideally be as diverse as possible,” says Pedersen. “High biodiversity is a sign of a healthy and resilient gut microbiome. And a healthy microbiome is not only essential for digestion and metabolism, it also plays an important role in immune function and brain health.” To understand the differences between vegans and omnivores, the researchers analyzed stool, blood, and urine samples. They then mapped the bacteria and viruses in the gut as well as signaling molecules in the body. “Apart from the reduced diversity of gut bacteria, we found that the vegans had a health-promoting gut microbiome,” says Pedersen. The vegans consumed more carbohydrates and dietary fiber and, on average, less protein and fat than the omnivores. They also had higher levels of several bacterial species capable of breaking down dietary fiber, along with a greater prevalence of the organism Blastocystis, which has been associated with lower blood pressure. The vegans also had lower blood glucose and cholesterol levels. Compared with the omnivores, they also had fewer inflammatory markers in the body. The researchers emphasize that the study is relatively small and observational comparing existing dietary patterns. The results may therefore point to associations, but they cannot establish whether specific dietary habits directly cause changes in the gut microbiome or to gut health, for example whether protein intake directly causes changes in gut biodiversity. As such, Pedersen cannot make dietary recommendations based on the new study. However, he says the findings support the importance of ensuring adequate nutrition, regardless of dietary preference: “Vegans in particular should consider whether they are getting enough protein in their diet, since they do not obtain it from meat, eggs, or dairy products. Good vegan sources of protein include beans, lentils, hemp seeds, chia seeds, quinoa, almonds, and nuts.” The research appears in Microbiome . Source: University of Copenhagen The post Vegan gut bacteria discovery surprises researchers appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Antibodies that coat the lining of your gut may be playing an important role in preventing colon cancer from developing, scientists have discovered. Mice that lack a specific class of antibodies, called immunoglobulin A (IgA), develop more than twice as many colon tumors as usual, the team reports in Nature . The study also explained why: When the antibodies bind to the cells lining the inside of the gut, it keeps those cells from dividing too quickly—which could lead to cancer. When the researchers gave IgA-deficient mice oral doses of the antibodies, they no longer had a higher risk of developing tumors. “One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer,” says senior author Daniel Mucida, head of Rockefeller University’s Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. “Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?” The discovery illuminates why people with IgA deficiency—who have few or none of these antibodies—are at a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer but also could shed light on other aspects of the complex interplay between the gut microbes, immune system, and cancer—even in otherwise healthy people. Scientists and clinicians have long known that the gut has high levels of IgA. Unlike many antibodies that are highly specific for one pathogen at a time, IgA is a broad-acting first line of defense in the immune system. A single IgA molecule can bind to a wide range of gut bacteria—as well as some healthy human cells—but researchers had long wondered why there were such high levels of IgA in the digestive system. Mucida and his colleagues study how the intestine strikes a balance between protecting the body against invading pathogens and absorbing the nutrients the body needs. In the past, for instance, the lab has discovered the role that gut immune cells play in food intolerances and allergies. In the new work, former Rockefeller postdoctoral fellow Gregory Donaldson—now an assistant professor at UCLA—wanted to tease out exactly how IgA antibodies interact with gut bacteria, and whether that could be relevant to colon cancer. “We know these antibodies bind bacteria and by doing so can shape the microbiome,” he says. “And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the US, is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease.” Donaldson began by studying IgA-deficient mice that were raised alongside normal mice, ensuring that they were exposed to the same germs and food. The mice without IgA developed more colorectal cancers than those who had IgA—echoing what was already known to occur in humans. “We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect,” says Donaldson. Moreover, giving these mice an oral treatment of IgA molecules eliminated the increased risk of cancer. Mucida, Donaldson, and the rest of their group zoomed in to the cells lining the gut, called epithelial cells—where colon cancers first form—to see how they were different in the mice lacking IgA. They discovered that changes in gene expression included ones related to cell division, or proliferation, and that these changes came before any tumors ever emerged. “We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this,” Donaldson says. Second author Gabriella Lima dos Reis, a graduate student in Gabriel Victora’s lab, homed in on one receptor that is found on the surface of epithelial cells and that IgA can bind to. Called DMBT1, it had already been linked in multiple ways to some cancers, but its exact role in colon cancer was unclear. The team went on to show that DMBT1, in the presence of gut bacteria, acts as a gas pedal for cell proliferation. But IgA, when it binds to DMBT1, acts as a brake. If IgA is completely absent, DMBT1 signaling is unrestrained, letting gut epithelial cells divide more than usual and form tumors. But without gut bacteria, without DMBT1 signaling, or with normal IgA levels, the epithelial cells are kept in check. “If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function—responding to bacteria by producing new cells—can keep dividing, leading to cancer,” Mucida says. “We think this homeostatic effect is IgA’s main function. This was a big surprise.” By establishing DMBT1’s natural function in epithelial cells for the first time, the findings may lay the groundwork for new interventions to reduce colon cancer risk. “Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor,” Mucida says. “We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point.” “What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well,” Donaldson notes. “A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it’s one direction that we could look toward in the future.” Mucida adds, “Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health.” Source: Rockefeller University The post Gut antibodies may help protect against colon cancer appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Types of Cycling Explained for Eco Riders and Race Followers Reading Time: 4 minutes From Daily Rides to Pro Races, Cycling Comes In Many Forms. Here’s a Simple Guide to Each One What Do You Mean by Cycling? Everyday Riding for a Greener Life The cost of gas and vehicle repairs and maintenance has many people looking at cycling as an alternative way to get around, but what do you mean by cycling exactly? Depending on where you’re cycling and your purpose for doing the activity, there are different types of cycling available for you. Some people are just looking to get places on main streets, while others are more adventurous and want to explore with off-road cycling. There are many different types of cycling , so let’s take a closer look at what the best might be for you. The Best Bicycle for Beginners So you think you want to give cycling a try. But what is the best bicycle for beginners ? As we already talked about, it really depends on the type of cycling you’re wanting to get into. There are many different types of cycling, and your equipment needs to fit the type that you are doing. Anyone who bikes regularly knows that each has its own needs, so your equipment needs to match where and how you’re going to be cycling. Different Types of Cycling: Road, Track, Mountain and More So what are the different types of cycling? There are many, as the sport has few limits on how you decide to approach it. For getting places and more relaxing rides, there is road cycling. This occurs – as the name implies – on roads, so there isn’t much terrain to worry about. The bike for road cycling is more sleek and aerodynamic, allowing for smoother rides on the smoother terrain that is being used. This leads to track cycling, where speed is more of a concern. The cycle and the attire of the cyclist are made for less wind resistance and greater speeds. Mountain biking comes with less predictable terrain, so the cycle itself must have more of a suspension system and wider tires to help the cyclist deal with the different obstacles that come up. There is less of a need for being aerodynamic with the cycle and the attire, since this type of cycling is more focused on getting through off-road trails. Another of the types of cycling is gravel cycling, which is a bit of a cross between mountain biking and road cycling. As you might guess, this type is on gravel trails, which brings fewer obstacles and a bit more stability on trails than mountain biking. The type of bike for this is a cross between mountain biking and road cycling, with wider tires but less suspension. A growing form of cycling is e-biking, which can be applied to almost any form of cycling. This is not a motorcycle or moped, as the cyclist still has to be doing work. The motor and battery on an e-bike assist when needed to make for longer rides and easier times for cyclists when they face obstacles like a steep climb. There are also racing forms of cycling, whether on streets like the Tour de France or over ramps and jumps in BMX racing. Types of Bicycle Racing in the Olympics When it comes to racing, the top venue for cycling is the Olympics. There are five different disciplines that are held in the Summer Olympic Games. Road cycling is done on outdoor courses with a mass-start road race. Also on outdoor courses is mountain bike racing, with rougher natural terrain, steep climbs, and obstacles. One of the more popular types of bicycle racing at the Olympics is track cycling, which is held on a banked oval track using fixed-gear bicycles with no brakes. There are multiple different events within this form of cycling, including team pursuit and sprints. There are two types of BMX racing in the Olympics as well. BMX racing is held on dirt tracks with as many as eight cyclists running the course filled with jumps and banked turns at a time. There is also BMX freestyle, which is a judged competition as riders perform tricks in a one-minute run on a park course. Bicycle Racing Categories Every Fan Should Know One of the most popular bicycle racing categories , or sporting events, in the world is the Tour de France, which is a stage race over multiple days that tests a cyclist’s endurance and strategy. Cyclists have stages that they complete each day, with the Tour de France having 21 stages over three weeks. It has made stars out of past winners like Greg LeMond and Lance Armstrong, and is also a big betting event for fans. Speaking of betting, you can see BetUS Sportsbook odds to win the 2027 Tour de France. There is also a form of racing called criteriums, which are shorter races in both distance and time but are just as spectator- and betting-friendly. These are often on street courses like auto racing, with the cyclists going around a track and past spectators. You can also find road races that are held over street courses for longer distances. These can be held with a mass start (everyone all at once), or in individual time trials where cyclists start in staggered intervals. FAQs What are the different types of cycling? There are many different types of cycling, from road cycling, mountain biking, gravel cycling, BMX cycling, e-biking, and track cycling. Which type of cycle is best for racing? The type of cycle needed for racing depends on the type of racing being done. Track or road cycling is different from off-road or BMX racing. Each type of racing requires a different kind of bicycle. How is a gravel bike different from a mountain bike? A gravel bike is made to be a combination of a mountain bike and a road bike, so it has the look of a road bike but the features of a mountain bike as well. They have wider tires and a more relaxed frame to give more versatility than a straight mountain bike. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Reading Time: 2 minutes PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Understanding Beverage Container Evolution The beverage packaging industry continually seeks materials that balance structural integrity, consumer appeal, and environmental responsibility. Producers must evaluate various packaging formats to meet shifting regulatory demands and sustainability targets. Two prominent contenders in modern production lines are the traditional metal cylinder and the transparent polymer vessel. Understanding their distinct characteristics regarding material recovery and mass reduction helps brand owners make informed decisions for their product portfolios. The Mechanics of Lightweighting Lightweighting remains a primary strategy for reducing transport emissions and material consumption. Aluminium packaging has historically achieved significant mass reduction through advanced wall-ironing techniques, resulting in thin, rigid walls that withstand internal pressure. On the other hand, the PET can offers unique advantages in mass optimization because polymer distribution can be precisely controlled during the stretch blow molding process. This allows manufacturers to tailor wall thickness to specific product requirements, whether packaging still water or carbonated beverages. Recycling Infrastructure and Material Recovery End-of-life processing heavily influences the overall sustainability footprint of any packaging format. Metal recycling systems are globally mature, allowing aluminium to be melted down repeatedly without losing its core mechanical properties. Polymer recovery has also advanced significantly, with dedicated sorting facilities capable of processing clear and colored containers efficiently. Both materials fit into circular economy models, though the specific infrastructure varies by geographic region. Key Production Considerations When selecting between these two packaging formats, producers must analyze several operational factors: Filling line compatibility and conversion costs for existing equipment Barrier properties required to protect product shelf life against oxygen and light Consumer perception of touch, transparency, and tactile experience Supply chain resilience and raw material price volatility Balancing Sustainability Goals Ultimately, the choice between metal and polymer containers depends on specific brand priorities and distribution models. While metal provides permanent recyclability, polymers offer design versatility and complete product visibility. By carefully assessing lightweighting potential and local recovery streams, producers can optimize their packaging strategy for long-term operational success. The post PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Take a walk through a city park. There are trees lining the paths, lawns stretching between them and plenty of shade. It looks green, perhaps even thriving. But where are the wild grasses that feed grazing animals? The flowering shrubs that attract butterflies? The ponds and stream banks where birds and other creatures find food and shelter? A place can look green while losing what wildlife needs to survive. That is the message emerging from Chandigarh's 2026 wildlife survey. Researchers recorded an impressive range of species, from a leopard and sambar deer to birds and butterflies. Yet they also found that several native trees were struggling to regenerate naturally and recommended greater protection for grasslands, wetlands and other habitats. For Indian cities, where planting drives often signal environmental progress, the findings suggest a better starting point: the habitat and the life it supports. What the survey found in Chandigarh's forests Conducted between 20 and 27 November 2025 by the Chandigarh Department of Forest and Wildlife and the Wildlife Institute of India (WII), the assessment covered Sukhna Wildlife Sanctuary and forest patches beyond its boundaries. Researchers documented 16 mammal species, 132 bird species, 73 butterfly species and 13 species of reptiles and amphibians. They also recorded 43 tree species, 14 shrub species and 22 herb species. The survey detected a leopard and estimated around 603 sambar, a deer species found in the region's forests. The figures show the variety of life these natural areas continue to shelter. But counting species was only one part of the exercise. The report also looked at the condition of their habitats and recommended restoring native vegetation, protecting grasslands, reviving wetlands and streamside habitats, and controlling invasive species. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Photograph: (The Tribune) Knowing which animals live in a forest matters. Knowing whether their habitat can continue to support them tells us what needs attention. A forest can have trees and still need help Imagine a woodland full of mature trees. From a distance, it might seem healthy. Look beneath the canopy, though, and there may be very few young trees coming up to replace the older ones. This is the problem of poor natural regeneration, which the Chandigarh survey flagged in native species including khair ( Senegalia catechu ), siris ( Albizia lebbeck ), Lannea coromandelica and Terminalia anogeissiana . Natural regeneration is simply the process of seeds becoming new plants without people planting them. It allows a forest to renew itself across generations. If young trees are missing, some native species could become less common as older trees die. That is why an increase in tree cover cannot, by itself, tell us whether a forest is doing well. The survey also cautioned against large plantations dominated by one species, known as monocultures. A row of identical trees may offer shade, but a healthy habitat needs different kinds of vegetation, from tall trees to shrubs, grasses and ground cover. Each layer has a purpose. Birds need places to nest, butterflies seek nectar, insects live among leaves and grasses, and herbivores depend on suitable plants for food. The report recommends replacing invasive vegetation with native species. Why does that matter? Why native plants can make a difference Native plants occur naturally in a region. Over time, they develop relationships with the insects, birds and animals around them. Some insects feed on particular plants; birds visit their flowers; other animals carry their seeds to new places. Introduced, or exotic, plants come from elsewhere. Many grow successfully in cities, and some offer flowers, fruit or shelter. But they do not always support the same relationships. Certain species can also spread so aggressively that they push out local vegetation. A 2023 Bengaluru study published in Science of the Total Environment helps explain why the distinction matters. Researchers compared how birds and mammals interacted with native and alien trees. They found that taller native trees with larger floral displays supported more bird species than alien trees with comparable displays. There was another interesting difference. Nectar-feeding birds were more likely to visit native flowers in ways that helped pollination. On alien trees, their visits more often involved 'nectar theft', where a bird takes nectar without transferring pollen in the way the flower needs to reproduce. This does not mean every introduced tree is harmful. The study recognised that alien trees can provide resources for wildlife in cities where natural vegetation has already been lost. The lesson is to understand what different plants actually offer local wildlife, rather than choosing them only because they grow quickly or look attractive. For Chandigarh, that supports the survey's recommendation to prioritise native vegetation that belongs to the landscape. Why an open grassland deserves protection A patch of tall, wild grass might look like an empty plot beside a landscaped park. It is easy to imagine someone deciding to plant trees there to 'improve' it. But a grassland is already a habitat. Its native grasses feed grazing animals, shelter insects and support species that depend on open spaces. Their roots also help hold soil together and influence how rainwater moves through the ground. Planting trees across an existing grassland can change the conditions that make it useful to those species. The result may look greener to us while offering less to the wildlife that lived there. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Photograph: (Chandigarh Help Post) This is why the Chandigarh survey specifically recommended protecting grasslands and restoring native grasses, including Eulaliopsis binata , Arundinella nepalensis and Heteropogon contortus . Across India, open spaces are often treated as land waiting to be developed, tidied up or planted over. Planners first need to ask what habitat is already there. Sometimes, caring for a green space means leaving room for its grasses to grow. Wetlands and riverbanks support different kinds of life The same principle applies to waterbodies and the land around them. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Woodland habitats, meanwhile, recorded the highest bird diversity. These differences matter. A forest, an open grassland and a stream bank may all be part of the same landscape, yet each offers food and shelter to different species. The report therefore called for wetland restoration and better care of streamside habitats , alongside other measures such as controlling invasive species. Research from the East Kolkata Wetlands shows why protecting such spaces requires attention to more than their size or appearance. A 2024 study in Environmental Research examined changes between 1991 and 2023. It found that the number of wetland patches had risen from 2,689 to 4,532, a sign that the landscape had become more fragmented. Over the same period, the study's ecosystem health index fell from 0.67 to 0.55. In simple terms, a wetland can still appear on a city map while its connected habitats are broken into smaller pieces and its ecological condition deteriorates. The Kolkata findings do not describe Chandigarh's wetlands, but they show what cities risk overlooking if they focus only on how much green or blue space remains. The two-day Capacity Building Workshop on Wildlife Survey & Techniques concluded today in Chandigarh! Diverse participants— representatives of civil society organisations, college students, wildlife enthusiasts, media personnel and journalists were sensitized and trained on various wildlife survey and monitoring methods. Thank all the multiple stakeholders for making it impactful. #WildlifeConservation #CitizenScience #WildlifeSurvey #Chandigarh #Sukhna #Chandigarhbirdclub @moefcc @wii_india @GobindsagarBha1 @RuchiBadola2 @gopigv @UDHAYAR230 @Ashik40405287 @Alexjacob11 @NonitaRana04 @RayR5847 — Wildlife Institute of India (@wii_india) November 19, 2025 Chandigarh's survey also recorded the red-eared slider turtle, an exotic aquatic species, and recommended its removal and management in controlled settings. Such species are sometimes released into waterbodies after being kept as pets and can place additional pressure on native wildlife. Wetlands need care as living habitats, not simply as water-filled spaces. What should other Indian cities measure? There is evidence from Delhi, too, that a park's value to wildlife depends on more than its tree count. A 2024 study in Ecological Frontiers examined birds across 64 city parks, recording 90 species and 19,131 individual birds. It found that vegetation characteristics and disturbance affected which birds used the parks. Native trees and lower surrounding urbanisation were also linked with greater bird diversity. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Chandigarh's plantation figures offer another lesson. During 2025–26, the administration planted 6,64,133 saplings against a target of 5,76,221. But third-party monitoring in November 2025 and March 2026 found an overall survival rate of around 79%. For 2026–27, the administration lowered its target to 4,19,854 saplings, including those distributed and sold, and said it would pay greater attention to site selection, quality and care after planting. Survival is important. So is asking whether the right species have been planted in the right place, and whether existing habitats are being protected rather than replaced. The Chandigarh survey was conducted over a short period, so its findings are a snapshot rather than proof that the city's wildlife populations are rising or falling. Longer-term, seasonal monitoring would help show how these habitats and their inhabitants change. But its message is already useful. Before the next plantation drive, city planners can ask a few practical questions: Is this land a forest, grassland or wetland? Which species rely on it? Are young native plants growing back? And what does this place need most? For some spaces, the answer will be trees. For others, it may be restoring a stream bank, protecting a grassland or allowing native shrubs to return. A city's natural wealth lives in more than its canopy. It is in the butterflies visiting riverbanks, the birds sheltering in woodland, the deer grazing on native grasses and the many smaller creatures that depend on them. Making room for all these habitats is how a city makes room for wildlife. Sources: 'Restore native species, wetlands; curb invasives: UT wildlife survey' : By Munieshwer A, Published on 2 October 2026 'Chandigarh's Wildlife Survey Exposes the Cost of Neglecting Native Habitats' : By Urban Acres, Published on 2 October 2026 'Urban park characteristics defining avian community structure in Delhi, India' : By Deepti Kumari, Ashutosh Srivastava, Upamanyu Hore, Published in December 2024 'Native fauna interact differently with native and alien trees in a tropical megacit' : By Purabi Deshpande, Rohan Sharma, Aleksi Lehikoinen, Rose Thorogood, Published on 10 April 2023 'Wildlife Week 2026 inaugurated in Chandigarh with Walkathon; focus on habitat connectivity and wildlife conservation' : By India News Calling, Published on 2 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: When people coined the proverb that “mighty oaks from little acorns grow”, they certainly weren’t thinking of Lyme disease. But literal acorns—not poetic metaphors—turn out to play a surprisingly big role in the spread of this mighty tick-borne illness, according to a recent paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . A surge in acorns one year can translate into a boom two years later in the population of ticks that transmit the disease to people. This discovery illustrates the ways in which a web of tiny, interconnected things—acorns, mice, microbes—can have big and unexpected consequences for people. It also shows that it can take decades of scientific research to decipher the head-scratching complexity of ecosystems. The results are “helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said Shannon LaDeau, one of the paper’s authors and an ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York State’s Hudson River Valley. LaDeau and colleague Richard Ostfeld oversee a Lyme-related research program at the institute that stretches back more than 30 years, just a few decades after the disease was first identified. Over that time, scientists have turned plots of New York forestland into an outdoor Lyme laboratory. They’ve assembled mountains of data tracking the ups and downs of a huge range of elements: temperature, rainfall, oak seedlings, mouse populations, tick numbers, infection rates, you name it. The results have repeatedly surprised scientists, defying expectations about the disease. It’s been known since the 1980s that the disease is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The bite of an infected deer tick transmits the bacterium to people, causing flu-like symptoms that can escalate to chronic fatigue, memory loss, depression and even brain swelling and cardiac problems. More than 450,000 cases are reported in the U.S. each year, plus more than 200,000 in Europe. Despite the tick’s association with deer, the Cary Institute work didn’t bear out initial suspicions that more white-tailed deer translated into more dangers for people. The researchers found no correlation between deer numbers and the abundance of tick nymphs—the life stage when they most commonly transmit the disease to people. Lyme Disease: Prescribed fire Instead, the researchers uncovered evidence of a cascade of cause and effect between oak trees, white-footed mice and ticks. Acorns from red oak trees at the study sites are a primary food source for the mice. The year after a big acorn harvest, the mouse population boomed, the scientists found. The mice, in turn, are a prime feeding target for larval ticks which go on to become nymphs the following year. A big year for mice translated into a roughly 40% increase in abundance of tick nymphs the next year. All this thanks to a bumper crop in acorns two years earlier. While acorns aren’t abundant everywhere that the disease occurs, fluctuations in other crucial mouse food, such as seeds, could have the same effect, the scientists wrote. While it took years to tease apart these dynamics, researchers were still puzzled by other patterns. A surge in mice meant more ticks—and therefore a greater risk of people getting infected. But it didn’t translate into a higher percentage of the ticks themselves carrying the disease, the data showed. “It kept me up at night,” Ostfeld said of the result. “It meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.” An apparent answer emerged when the researchers looked not just at the mouse population, but at a variety of small mammals. The long-term study plots were located in relatively intact forest that supported a range of other warm-blooded critters, such as skunks, squirrels and opossums. Many of these creatures are less prone to getting infected when a tick feeds on them, which also means they are less likely to spread the bacteria to other ticks. As a consequence, the percentage of infected ticks was driven not just by the number of mice but the population of a range of creatures. By contrast, in nearby places where forests had been broken into pieces by human intrusion , the diversity of small mammals was smaller. In those spots, where ticks had fewer options, higher mouse numbers did translate into more infected ticks. So in addition to small things like acorns, add two very big things that shape people’s risk of encountering Lyme disease: loss of habitat and of biodiversity. Ostfeld, et. al. “ The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis .” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , Aug. 17, 2026. Image:© Theclarkester | Dreamstime.com

items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, once the paddy harvest is over, farmers across Haryana face a familiar problem. Their fields are covered with leftover straw, and they need to clear the land before planting the next crop. For many, burning this stubble is the quickest solution. But the smoke that rises from these fields adds to North India's already severe air pollution. Now imagine if that same straw could earn money, create jobs and even help power industries. That's exactly what two women from Haryana and neighbouring Rajasthan set out to do. Sanjana, a graduate from Ghoranwali village in Haryana's Sirsa district, and her friend Sonika, from Bhadra in Rajasthan, saw a business opportunity in something farmers struggled to get rid of. They decided to collect leftover paddy straw , locally called parali , and turn it into biofuel pellets that power plants could use as an alternative fuel. In 2024, they started SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore. Today, the venture reports an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore and employs over 20 people. From a pollution problem to a business idea For Sonika, the idea began with a sight she had witnessed repeatedly after the paddy harvest: thick smoke spreading across the sky as farmers burned crop residue. Concerned about the environmental and public health consequences, she began thinking about how this agricultural waste could be put to better use. Rather than treating stubble burning as a problem with no easy solution, she and Sanjana started exploring ways to convert the residue into a commercially useful product. At their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali, Haryana, machinery processes leftover paddy straw into compact biofuel pellets, giving agricultural waste a productive use. Photograph: ( Peddler media ) The idea was to address two needs together: give farmers a productive use for their leftover crop residue while creating an alternative fuel that industries could use. Government policies and initiatives promoting stubble management also helped create an opportunity for the venture to take shape. Building a factory around farm waste In 2024, Sanjana and Sonika set up their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) scheme. The factory follows a process that begins in the fields. The women source paddy straw through baler operators in Sirsa and surrounding areas. These operators collect and compress the loose residue, making it easier to transport and store. The stubble is then brought to their factory, where machinery processes it into compact biofuel pellets. These pellets can be supplied to power plants as an alternative fuel. By sourcing paddy straw from farmers and baler operators across the region, the founders are creating a market for crop residue. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The scale of the operation is considerable. The unit uses approximately 1 lakh to 1.5 lakh quintals of paddy stubble every year. Since the raw material is available mainly during the harvesting season, the founders also have to plan for the months ahead. They collect and store the residue after harvest, ensuring that the factory has enough raw material to continue production throughout the year. This seasonal sourcing and year-round production model allows them to keep the business running beyond the harvesting window. From discarded straw to a growing rural enterprise The venture's impact extends beyond the pellets it produces. By creating a market for paddy straw, SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited also generates business opportunities for local baler operators and others involved in collecting and transporting the residue. The factory itself provides employment to more than 20 people, bringing work opportunities closer to home for residents in and around the village. From an initial investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore, Sanjana and Sonika have built an enterprise reporting an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore. What began as an effort to address stubble burning has grown into a rural enterprise that employs over 20 people and reports an annual turnover of Rs 8 crore. Photograph: ( Peddler Media ) For the two founders, the next harvest season will bring another opportunity to source more stubble, keep production going and expand their business. Their work has given farmers in the region another possible route for managing crop residue, while creating a market for material that would otherwise have little economic value. In Ghoranwali, the paddy harvest no longer marks just the end of a farming cycle. For Sanjana and Sonika, it also marks the beginning of another season of business, one built around putting farm waste to productive use. Sources: '2 women turn paddy stubble into Rs 8-crore business in Haryana' by Anil Kakkar for The Tribune, Published on 14 October 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: A road outside a forest stays lit after sunset. So does a nearby place of worship or a cluster of shops where people gather. Those lights help people go about their lives. But their glow can travel beyond the places they are meant to illuminate. For wildlife living in Kerala's Western Ghats, that raises an important question: how much of the night inside protected forests is still naturally dark? A team of four researchers has begun answering it. Their study, published in Biological Conservation in October 2026, mapped artificial light in and around 21 protected areas in Kerala and examined the roads, buildings and other human activities associated with it. Their findings reveal a conservation concern that is easy to overlook: even where forests have protected boundaries, light from surrounding areas can still reach them. What's causing the forests to light up? Using satellite data from 2024, researchers S. Haripriya, M.S. Arjun, S. Gopakumar and Vijayan Divya measured night-time light across national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. They then compared those measurements with maps showing nearby roads, places of worship, buildings and centres of human activity. The difference between forests was striking. Periyar Tiger Reserve's western division recorded the highest average and peak levels of satellite-measured light among the 21 areas, with a mean radiance of 0.369 and a maximum of 24.0. Kerala's protected areas include tropical evergreen forests, semi-evergreen forests, shola-grassland ecosystems and riverine habitats. Photograph: (Tiger Safari Tours India) Within protected areas, the strongest statistical link was with the density of places of worship. In the surrounding landscape, road networks and places where people gather or work were more important predictors. That distinction matters. Light affecting a forest may be associated with several kinds of human activity, and managing it requires knowing where to look. But light does not always arrive as a visible beam. It can scatter through the atmosphere and brighten the night sky over places some distance away. Researchers call this skyglow . The team examined areas extending up to 30 km beyond forest boundaries. Their modelling suggested that the wider surrounding landscape, particularly the 10–30 km zone, could contribute substantially to skyglow. This means lighting decisions made several kilometres away may influence how dark a protected forest remains at night. Why does darkness matter to wildlife? The Western Ghats are home to many species found nowhere else, including animals active after dark. Natural cycles of light and darkness help wildlife navigate, find food and follow daily rhythms. Research elsewhere has shown that artificial lighting can alter animal behaviour. However, the Kerala study did not directly observe animals or measure how they were affected. That distinction is important. The researchers have identified where artificial light is present and which features of the surrounding landscape are associated with it. Understanding what those light levels mean for different species will require further research. Lead author S. Haripriya has also expressed an interest in investigating these ecological effects in future. Could simple lighting changes help protect these forests? For forest departments and local authorities, the study offers something immediately useful: a way to identify areas where lighting deserves closer attention. A brightly lit road near a forest edge could be assessed for lamps that shine upwards or sideways. Places of worship and tourism facilities could review whether lights need to remain on at full strength throughout the night. Shielded fixtures, lower-intensity lighting and switching off unnecessary lights during periods of low activity are among the options worth considering, while keeping public safety in mind. Periyar Tiger Reserve's western division recorded the highest average and peak levels of satellite-measured light among the 21 areas, with a mean radiance of 0.369 and a maximum of 24.0. Photograph: (Deccan Herald) These are possible next steps rather than changes already implemented because of the study. The findings could, however, help forest officials, local communities and those responsible for public lighting decide where action would be most useful. For years, protecting forests has meant paying attention to what happens within their boundaries. This research offers a reason to look beyond those boundaries, too. And sometimes, protecting a forest's natural environment may begin with something as simple as reconsidering where, when and how we use light. Sources: 'Spatial assessment of artificial light at night in and around protected areas of the Kerala Western Ghats' : By S. Haripriya, M.S. Arjun, S. Gopakumar and Vijayan Divya 'From illumination expansion to ecological response: artificial light at night and detectability of forest vegetation responses across India' : By Dibyendu Dutta, Published on 31 October 2026 'New study examines effect of artificial light at night in protected areas' : By Arathi Menon, Published on 5 November 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: A patch of dust near a busy road, smoke rising from an industrial chimney, and waste burning in an open space may all contribute to a city's air pollution. But the sources responsible for poor air quality are not necessarily the same across neighbourhoods. This means that a measure addressing pollution in one part of a city may not be equally effective elsewhere. Understanding what contributes to poor air quality at specific locations is therefore an important part of planning cleaner cities . Ahmedabad is attempting to address this challenge by looking beyond citywide air-quality readings and examining pollution at specific locations. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring initiative called SMART-VAYU. Reported by The Times of India (TOI) on September 30, 2026, the project aims to identify local pollution hotspots, trace the sources of emissions and generate data that can help civic authorities plan targeted interventions. Initial monitoring exercises at two locations — Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium — have already revealed how pollution sources can differ within the same city. One city, two different pollution profiles The initial findings from Ahmedabad offer an interesting look at how the sources contributing to air pollution can vary from one location to another. In its October 17, 2026 report, TOI detailed the findings from air-quality sampling at the Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium. Sampling at the riverfront was conducted between May 4 and May 24, while monitoring at Narendra Modi Stadium took place between June 25 and August 8. At the Sabarmati Riverfront, dust accounted for 36% of the estimated source contribution, compared with 23% at Narendra Modi Stadium. Coal combustion contributed 24% at the riverfront, while its estimated contribution at the stadium was just 1%. The pattern was different at Motera. The combined category of marine emissions and refuse burning accounted for 38% of the estimated pollution sources at Narendra Modi Stadium, compared with 16% at the riverfront. Power plant-related sources contributed another 20% at the stadium. The analysis also examined different types of organic aerosols. Traffic-related organic aerosols contributed 18% at Narendra Modi Stadium and 13% at the riverfront. Solid-fuel combustion-related organic aerosols accounted for 16% at the stadium and 5% at the riverfront. These findings highlight an important aspect of urban air pollution: even within one city, different locations can have different pollution profiles . Understanding these differences can help authorities identify which sources need attention in specific areas, rather than approaching air pollution as a uniform problem across the city. Why Ahmedabad is looking beyond citywide AQI readings Identifying the sources behind air pollution is not always straightforward. Citywide air-quality readings provide information about pollution levels, but understanding what is contributing to poor air quality in a particular neighbourhood requires more detailed monitoring. This is the gap that SMART-VAYU aims to address. The initiative stands for Sensing and Monitoring for Air Quality using Real-time Technology – Vision-based Ahmedabad air analysis for Urban Management. The project involves three broad components: mapping existing pollution sources, establishing a hyperlocal monitoring network and developing a decision-support system for urban air-quality management. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. Photograph: (Ahmedabad Mirror) For this, AMC and IIT Kanpur finalised 10 monitoring locations across Ahmedabad. These include Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex, Narendra Modi Stadium, Gujarat Police Academy at Karai, Sanskardham, Veer Savarkar Sports Complex, Pirana AMC community service centre, Rakhial AMC health office, Vatva GIDC's Chandrakala complex, Bopal urban health centre and Thaltej AMC ward office. The selection considered meteorological conditions, particulate matter readings, annual wind patterns, satellite-based aerosol optical depth and estimated PM2.5 concentrations. Practical requirements such as electricity, security, accessibility and airflow were also taken into account. The plan is to deploy five locations with mobile laboratory sampling alongside sensors, while the remaining five will have fixed sensors. The wider project envisages eventually expanding the network to around 400 sensors across Ahmedabad. How the monitoring network will identify pollution sources Unlike conventional monitoring systems that primarily provide broader air-quality readings, these sensors will continuously measure pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide. They will also record meteorological parameters, including temperature and humidity. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring. Photograph: (Hindustan Times) An important component is the mobile Real-Time Source Apportionment Laboratory (RTSA), which will help examine the contribution of different pollution sources. Source apportionment is the process of estimating how much different sources contribute to the pollutants present in the air. These could include vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road dust, construction and waste burning. By examining these contributions, the initiative aims to generate pollution hotspot maps, forecasts and alerts that can help authorities identify locations requiring attention. From identifying pollution to planning targeted action Ahmedabad already has an air-quality monitoring network under the Centre's System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research (SAFAR) programme. Its monitoring stations provide city-level air-quality information and forecasts. SMART-VAYU seeks to add another layer of information by examining pollution sources at specific locations. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. For instance, identifying road dust as a major contributor could inform dust-control and road-cleaning measures. Similarly, evidence of industrial emissions or waste burning could help direct inspections and enforcement. The effectiveness of the initiative will depend on how consistently the monitoring network operates, whether its findings translate into enforceable measures and how improvements in air quality are tracked over time. Ultimately, Ahmedabad's initiative highlights why tackling urban air pollution requires more than understanding how polluted a city is. It also requires knowing what is polluting different parts of it. Because when pollution sources vary from one neighbourhood to another, the solutions must account for those differences too. Sources: 'Ahmedabad: SMART-VAYU to zoom in on air pollution hotspots' : By Kapil Dave, Published on 30 September 2026 'Ahmedabad maps pollution hotspots ahead of 2030 Commonwealth Games' : By Meghdoot Sharon, Published on 17 October 2026 'IIT-K Ahmedabad Gets Real-Time Pollution Tracking Activity' : By Kotak School of Sustainability - IIT Kanpur

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Students Giving Tennis a Second Serve Reading Time: 4 minutes A student-run nonprofit born in Flower Mound, Texas, now keeps used tennis balls out of landfills in 16 states. A single tennis ball weighs about two ounces. That is easy to overlook, because nobody throws away just one. Since 2024, BallBack , a student-led nonprofit based in Flower Mound, Texas, has recycled or repurposed more than 160,000 of them. At roughly 58 grams apiece, that is about 9.3 metric tons of rubber and felt, a little over 20,000 pounds. Every one of those balls was headed for the trash. According to RecycleBalls, a tennis ball takes roughly 400 years to break down, slowly shedding microplastics into the surrounding soil. Curbside recycling programs do not accept them. The national picture is larger still. The United States discards an estimated 125 million tennis balls each year, or about 340,000 a day. By comparison, 160,000 balls is less than half a day of the country’s tennis ball waste. What makes BallBack interesting is not only its total so far, but how quickly a model built by high school students is spreading, and how easily it can be copied by anyone with a court, a school, and a car. BallBack began with Prem Kamasani, a varsity tennis player at Flower Mound High School. After practice one evening, he watched his coach getting ready to throw out roughly 400 used balls. He asked whether he could take them instead. “I noticed hundreds of balls going to the trash every week, and no one was doing anything about it,” Kamasani says on BallBack’s website. The balls went home with him. Some went to animal shelters as toys, and others ended up under school chairs. He then began calling local tennis centers to ask whether they had balls to give away as well. Most did. The collection outgrew his family’s garage, then several garages, and teammates joined in. A Lead4Change grant helped turn the school project into a national organization, spreading to over 310 members in 2026. The funding covered prepaid shipping, so courts anywhere in the country could send in their balls at no cost. Partnerships spread across Dallas–Fort Worth, from public facilities such as Kiest and Samuell Grand tennis centers to SMU’s college tennis program and the Flower Mound Animal Shelter. BallBack’s process is deliberately simple. A chapter leader places a free, branded collection bin at a partner facility, such as a tennis center, club, school, or homeowners’ association. Players drop off dead balls after practice instead of tossing them in the trash. Nobody on site has to sort or clean anything. Leaders monitor fill levels and stop by once or twice a month before anything overflows. Recycling bins at Samuell Grand Tennis Center in Dallas, one of BallBack’s partner facilities, let players drop off used tennis balls instead of throwing them away. Photo courtesy of BallBack . Sorting comes next, and it reflects the organization’s priorities. Balls that still bounce are never shredded. They go back into play through youth tennis programs and school teams that cannot afford new equipment, as well as other repurposing partners. Others go to dog shelters as enrichment toys, or to senior living communities, where they serve as walker feet. BallBack boxes only the balls with no play left in them, labels them with prepaid UPS shipping, and sends them to RecycleBalls or the USTA, BallBack’s national recycling partners. There, they separate the rubber and felt and grind them into crumb rubber that becomes new tennis court surfaces, playground padding, and footing for equestrian arenas. Through RecycleBalls and USTA, BallBack’s shipments help feed a North American collection network of roughly 10,000 locations. BallBack now runs with a national team of students recruited from across the country, each responsible for a distinct part of the work. The media team shapes how BallBack tells its story, from pickup-day footage to chapter spotlights. The marketing team carries that story to new schools, players, and facilities. The onboarding team brings each new chapter leader up to speed with step-by-step guides, so a student in Seattle or Fort Lauderdale can complete a first pickup within a week of signing up. Leaders trade questions and progress in a shared online community. This structure lets the network grow without relying on any one person. BallBack now counts 31 student chapter leaders across 16 states, more than 310 members, and over 55 partner facilities. Chapters operate in New York City, Philadelphia, Chicago, Portland, Seattle, Minneapolis, Folsom, and Green Bay, among other cities. In Manhattan, one senior ships roughly 750 balls a month. In Falls Church, Virginia, chapter leader Surya Arivumani has already recycled more than 1,200. BallBack is set up so that taking part does not depend on where you live. High school sophomores, juniors, and rising seniors in any U.S. city without an existing chapter can apply to start one at their local school. The commitment is one or two pickup trips a month, an hour or two each, for at least four months. Costs are close to zero, and leaders unlock $60 in credit after their first shipment. New chapter leaders are accepted every quarter. Tennis facilities near an existing chapter can list themselves as operating partners and receive free bins, pickups, and shipping. Facilities elsewhere can join as affiliate partners and ship their own boxes for free using prepaid FedEx labels. Individuals with a bag of old balls in the garage can also request a free shipping label, pack a box, and drop it off at FedEx. In Dallas–Fort Worth, anyone with 100 or more balls can arrange a free pickup. BallBack’s next milestone is a world record for the most tennis balls recycled in a single week. The plan is a coordinated national recycling week in spring of 2027. Chapter leaders, members, and partner facilities nationwide would collect, sort, and ship tennis balls at the same time. The effort is still being organized, as BallBack has yet to choose an adjudicator to set the rules for counting and verifying the balls. Whatever the final tally, the week is designed to do what no single chapter can: show what happens when hundreds of courts in dozens of cities choose to recycle at once. Long before BallBack, Kamasani’s father sent him to gather old balls from behind their neighborhood courts instead of buying new ones. Today, Kamasani mentors student leaders he’s never met in cities he’s never visited, who are doing the same thing on a national scale. In BallBack’s latest milestone update, he wrote that the 160,000 mark showed what “a bin by the fence and a student with a car” can accomplish. Students interested in starting a chapter, facilities that want to host a bin, and players with balls to donate can find details at ballback.org . The post The Students Giving Tennis a Second Serve appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Japanese Scientists Design a Plant-Based Plastic that can Become Fertilizer Reading Time: 3 minutes Researchers at Chiba University have developed a flexible, plant-based plastic that can be turned into crop fertilizer after use. Plant-based plastic often ends up in the same places as ordinary plastic, from landfills to incinerators. A research team in Japan wants to give it a more useful ending. What if a used plastic film could help grow the next crop? Associate Professor Daisuke Aoki of Chiba University led the study . Colleagues from the University of Tokyo and Tohoku University joined the work. They published their results in the journal Scientific Reports in August 2026. The need for new ideas is growing. Global plastic use reached 460 million metric tons in 2019, according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. If current trends continue, it could climb to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060. Recycling and waste-to-energy plants are struggling to keep pace with this growth. Aoki’s team took a different route by designing a plastic with its end-of-life already planned. The material starts with isosorbide, a nontoxic compound made from glucose. Glucose is a simple sugar that can come from plant starch, such as corn. Chemists link isosorbide units into a clear, hard plastic called poly(isosorbide carbonate). In 2021, Aoki and his students showed that warm ammonia water breaks down this plastic. The process splits it back into isosorbide and urea. Urea is one of the world’s most widely used nitrogen fertilizers. Aoki compared the goal to the Haber-Bosch process, which turned nitrogen from the air into fertilizer a century ago. His team hoped to turn plastic waste into food in a similar way. Their conversion also needed no costly metal catalysts. One problem remained. The original plastic was hard and brittle, stretching only about 4% before it snapped. That limited it to a narrow range of rigid products. Most plastics are softened with additives called plasticizers. Common ones, such as phthalates, do not break down into anything useful. Some also raise health concerns. The Chiba team designed a plasticizer for its plant-based plastic from the same building block. It has an isosorbide core linked to two short triethylene glycol chains, a common industrial chemical. Like the plastic, it breaks apart when treated with ammonia. With the new plasticizer, the material stretched about 45% before breaking, more than ten times as far as before. It also began to soften at about 40 degrees Celsius instead of 161 degrees, a sign of greater flexibility. Unlike a phthalate blend, the new mix stayed clear and uniform at every mixing ratio. The phthalate version turned cloudy, indicating its ingredients had separated. The team also made a longer-chain version of the plasticizer that stretched the plastic even further. It could be made at yields above 80%, versus under 25% for the first version. That makes it more practical to produce at scale. Converting the used plastic is simple. The team heated it in ammonia water at 90 degrees Celsius for 24 hours. The solid plastic dissolved completely into a clear liquid. That liquid held most of the original building blocks. The team recovered about 98% of the isosorbide, 78% of the possible urea, and 90% of the glycol. Some carbon escaped as carbon dioxide, and better conditions could raise the urea yield. Next came the most important test. The researchers used the liquid as fertilizer without any purification. They tried it on a common lab plant and on komatsuna, a leafy green often called Japanese mustard spinach. Over 36 days in a greenhouse, komatsuna grown with the recycled product matched plants fed commercial urea. Both groups grew far better than plants given no nitrogen. In the lab, the product performed at least as well as urea alone. Komatsuna grown with fertilizer from recycled plant-based plastic matched plants fed commercial urea. Photo courtesy of Scientific Reports . The authors are clear about the limits. Their plant-based plastic is not biodegradable, so it only becomes fertilizer after chemical treatment. Its strength is also not yet high enough for demanding uses. Other questions remain open. The team has not yet tested whether the plasticizer leaks out over time. They also have not measured the full energy cost and environmental footprint of the conversion process. Even so, the researchers see clear uses ahead. This plant-based plastic could be used for agricultural mulch films, seedling pots, shopping bags, and packaging. Farms could then turn used films and pots into fertilizer on site. Aoki believes plastics are at a turning point. He hopes people will one day see plastic waste as a valuable resource for growing food rather than trash. If that happens, plant-based plastic could complete a full circle. Plant-based material would return to the soil to feed new plants. The post Japanese Scientists Design a Plant-Based Plastic that can Become Fertilizer appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: “Just eat less.” “Work harder.” “Have some willpower.” We hear it all the time. But if weight loss were that simple, why can keeping it off feel even harder? Because sometimes, your own biology pushes back. After you lose weight, your body can respond with stronger hunger signals and lower energy use. These biological adaptations can favour weight regain. Does that mean weight always comes back? No. It means long-term medical support may need more than a short burst of willpower. And struggling doesn’t mean someone is lazy or lacks discipline. Weight is shaped by biology, behaviour and environment. If you keep struggling, continue with practical nutrition, movement, strength and sleep habits. And if weight repeatedly returns, or the plan feels impossible to sustain, speak to a qualified doctor about long-term weight management and the biological or practical barriers involved. Getting medical support is not failure. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight management. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightRegain #WeightManagement #Biology #HealthJourney [why weight comes back after weight loss, body pushes back after weight loss, hunger signals and weight regain, struggling with weight is not a character flaw, India]

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Get smart Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans. Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. Will says: As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. Mapping roots In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. “I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” Becca says: On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable tree. On the other hand, I do like the idea of people detouring to see cool trees . What else we’re reading Minnesota announces ‘effective end’ to veteran homelessness, achieving decades-long goal — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from KSTP Free tool helps young men to take responsibility for sexual harm — shared by Contributing Editor Geetanjali Krishna from Positive News ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis? — shared by Michaela Haas from the Guardian In other news… Turns out people love moss! Our Instagram video about how moss is taking over cities has really taken off. To learn more about all the cool things moss can do, read Michaela Haas’s great story. The post What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: At fourteen, Shakhzoda Saidova slipped away from a conference table with the UN General Assembly and UNICEF in Tajikistan — too nervous, too convinced she didn't belong. What brought her back was a single sentence from a mentor: stay true to what you're actually hearing from inside. That line has followed her into every room since. She grew up in a country where her mother — who finished school with perfect marks and won a law scholarship — was forbidden by her husband's family from ever practicing as a lawyer. Watching that buried ambition became Shakhzoda's compass. Now studying in Romania, she is building SafeVoice: a disarmingly simple website listing real lawyers and crisis shelter numbers for women in Tajikistan facing domestic violence, because she knows what it costs a woman with three children and one free minute to find a page of dead links. She speaks five languages and is already being criticized for living in Europe at nineteen instead of being married. What's striking is the image of her mother, smiling serenely at those who disapprove — "Yes, I allowed that; yes, she's my daughter" — after accepting her daughter's diploma while the teenager boarded a flight towards a future she herself was never allowed to choose.
