items.descriptionOriginal: W hat might it be like to be a bird? Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles. “Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough grassland in which to hunt voles and mice, and space undisturbed by people and dogs. Suddenly the landscape around Lawy looked more like a series of obstacles and threats a wild animal needed to conquer: “Once I really began to delve into what it might be like to be a kestrel, I realized actually my options were very limited because it’s so difficult to find areas where I can find food.” Clatworthy dam impounds the headwaters of the River Tone. © River Tone Lawy’s experience is part of a pioneering experiment by Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment (ASRA), an independent nonprofit initiative hosted by the United Nations Foundation in collaboration with the University of the West of England (UWE) and funded by the Ecological Citizen(s) Network . The project, Risks Beyond Human Eyes, asks people around the River Tone catchment to explore risks not from the conventional perspective of human visitors, landowners, planners or conservationists, but through the sensory worlds and needs of other species: fierce otter, threatened salmon, quiet red deer, sharp-sighted kestrel or blind earthworm. Over a period of several months, 18 participants swam like salmon, surfed the river to mimic how an otter might glide through the water, or hid in hollows like earthworms. The setup sounds fanciful until its practical implications emerge: If conventional risk assessments systematically overlook what matters to other species, could temporarily shifting the human viewpoint reveal problems — and solutions — that would otherwise remain invisible? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] For Lawy, it has already changed how she manages land. She came to the project as a local resident, concerned about the water quality of the River Tone. People want to bathe in it, yet the water is too polluted with runoff from the nearby fields, herbicides, pesticides and other toxins. “But animals haven’t got that choice,” she says. “They are constantly living in this very poor-quality water.” These insights are part of the logic of the ASRA project, challenging the human-centeredness of conventional risk assessment. “Of course we’re not pretending that a person literally becomes an otter or kestrel,” project co-director Phil Tovey explains, “but this kind of disciplined attention exposes aspects of an animal’s environment that humans routinely fail to notice.” The resulting testimonies are not intended simply to produce moving stories about wildlife, but are treated as input to a wider systemic-risk assessment, alongside scientific and other evidence such as water quality. Participants in the project working on a course of action. Credit: Darren Honeywell According to the 2026 Living Planet Index , freshwater species populations declined by 85 percent between 1970 and 2022 , the steepest decline of any of the major ecosystems assessed. It’s one thing to read this number as an intellectual piece of information and another to attempt the perspective of a salmon, like some of the study participants, and arrive at the life-threatening realization that they couldn’t overcome a river barrier to get to their food source. Lawy experienced firsthand that a landscape designed to look accessible and attractive to humans appears radically different to a species trying to feed and reproduce. While repeatedly sitting outside over several weeks, Lawy never actually saw a kestrel. There were too many people, too many dogs, too much disturbance. “Kestrels actually need some space from us,” she realized. Lawy also saw the hay meadows in a different light. Once the hay is cut, Lawy suddenly noticed, the landscape can become a stark, hostile expanse. “There is no cover,” she says. During a hot, dry summer, that lack of shelter can mean the difference between life and death. At the next meeting of Friends of Longrun Meadow, Lawy proposed a “mosaic of habitats,” retaining more long grass and larger riparian margins alongside the river instead of the more manicured grounds. The River Tone under the M5. © River Tone Lawy says she now asks people to adopt a new perspective. “I want you to think more from an animal perspective,” she tells them. “Rather than us thinking we need to trim that hedge, are we leaving places for birds and insects and all these other species who live here? Are we providing feeding corridors for bats?” Much to her surprise, the group “straightforwardly accepted these insights,” Lawy reports. The larger ambition of ASRA’s experiment is to translate these observations into protective action. Phil Tovey, who co-leads the project with Miguel Prado Casanova of UWE, describes the River Tone as a system in which risks compound. For instance, research has found that kestrels living within 30 meters of a major road show elevated cortisol from stress, and they shift from reproduction towards survival. “So when we then look at overall coverage of roads in the region, you can just see the scale of harm, disruption, physical and mental injury that is really widespread,” Tovey concludes. “One of the things that we do in ASRA for a systemic risk response is we look at the underlying structures, the historical conditions and what are the barriers to transformation.” A former Royal Marines Commando, Tovey served on operations across the world, from peacekeeping in Northern Ireland to working with indigenous forces in Afghanistan and deployments across Africa and the Middle East. Before joining ASRA, he worked as the Head of Futures in the U.K.’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Rain patters downstream of French Weir. © River Tone He likens the emotional testimonies of the study participants to the shocked reports of civilians caught in war zones. He also conducted roughly two dozen of his own field experiments, switching between species and testing the instructions given to participants. “I’d be going out at four in the morning, roughly knowing where the red deer hang out.” For Tovey, connecting the participants’ testimonies to scientific evidence and a structured framework for mapping risk means “setting the conditions for deeper structural change.” For example, the river and its tributaries contain more than 337 weirs and other obstacles over about 33 kilometers, creating problems for migrating salmon and other creatures. “No one has really considered the density and volume of these pressures on the animals,” Tovey says. “But when I sit as an otter, I see these barriers because as an otter I’m only about six centimeters off the ground.” Conventional assessments tend to divide problems into categories: transport, agriculture, water quality, habitat, biodiversity. Tovey’s digital mapping of the River Tone risks is effectively “bright orange” as different risks overlap. The problem is not merely the number of individual hazards, but their density and interaction. Changing the perspective does not mean abandoning scientific evidence, but it can show which actions will have the most impact. “As a research team, asking a bunch of humans to try and inevitably fail to engage in living as a chosen animal, the absurdity of trying to actually do that was taken really seriously,” says Tovey, addressing the obvious criticism of anthropomorphism. “We never once claimed that Helen was a kestrel, but using the structured process we set out, we need to make an imaginary leap to calibrate what that environment would be like for the animal. Then we start to see barriers in a different way.” The research team briefing the Systemic Risk Assessment. Credit: Darren Honeywell For Lawy, the exercise in changing perspective led to changes in land management, and then to a recognition that she wants to press for changes beyond her local group. “It’s amazing how quickly that local action on a relatively small area can lead you to realize that actually we need some policy changes within the landscape to really make that difference,” she says. The project inspired an even more ambitious question: What does the river need? One of the study participants works in the city council. According to Tovey, “she became instrumental in stitching together the work and applying it to River Tone as a subjective person.” A working group quickly formed, resulting in the adaptation of Somerset’s very first River Rights Charter, which recognizes the river’s rights to regenerate, flow and be protected from harm. Lawy’s stint as a kestrel is part of a growing global movement to shift from an anthropocentric view, inspired by programs such as NYU Law School’s More than Human Life as well as bestselling authors like Charles Foster , whose book Being A Beast portrayed him living as badger, deer, fox and swift. It also marks a return to Indigenous values. In 2008, Indigenous peoples led Ecuador to become the world’s first country to formally recognize the “Rights of Mother Earth,” a ruling that the Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature (GARN) and others subsequently used successfully against a road construction company that dumped rubble into the Vilcabamba River. As a result, the government was forced to clean up the river. Tovey agrees that rivers and other elements of nature should have the right to be represented. “I have never met my MP,” he says. “Yet we accept political representation for humans. What’s problematic is making sure it’s done with integrity.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The approach remains experimental. There are obvious limits to humans attempting to understand other species, and the researchers themselves acknowledge the need for more time. But Tovey hopes to expand ASRA’s work to larger areas. “We have started to forge connections with our sister rivers, reaching out to those groups and thinking about a wider solidarity movement,” Tovey says, intending to integrate the lessons from the River Tone project. Lawy’s experience suggests another potential benefit: changing what people care about. “One of the really important things that’s come out of this for me,” she says, “is the emotional connection that you get back with nature.” That emotional connection is not taken as a substitute for evidence. Rather, it can make evidence harder to ignore. The post The People Who Became Wildlife appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Results-Based Conservation Finance in Africa Gets a $4.6 Million Boost Reading Time: 3 minutes A new $4.6 million commitment from the Rob Walton Foundation is testing whether results-based conservation finance in Africa can tie funding directly to verified outcomes across four protected areas. Results-based conservation finance in Africa took a significant step forward with a new $4.6 million commitment from the Rob Walton Foundation. The funding flows to African Parks, a nonprofit that manages protected areas across the continent. Unlike a typical grant, payment is tied directly to verified conservation outcomes rather than activities alone. The deal relies on a tool called the Verifiable Nature Unit (VNU), which African Parks and The Landbanking Group developed together starting in 2024. Each unit represents one square kilometer of land where ecological integrity has been maintained or improved over a year. Independent verification confirms whether that standard has actually been met before funding is released. Funding under this agreement will support four protected areas spread across very different parts of the continent. Majete Wildlife Reserve in Malawi, Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo, Garamba National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Zakouma National Park in Chad will all benefit. The money will support biodiversity monitoring, community development projects, and park infrastructure. Each of these four parks faces its own mix of challenges, from poaching pressure to limited local infrastructure and competing land uses nearby. Community development funding is meant to give nearby residents a stake in keeping ecosystems intact, through jobs, services, or shared benefits tied to the park’s success. Supporters of the VNU model argue that linking funding directly to measurable outcomes could eventually make that kind of community investment more consistent across very different park settings. African Parks has already issued VNUs covering a combined 1.37 million hectares across three of these parks in 2025 and 2026. That scale makes the current grant one of the larger tests yet of whether outcomes-based payment can work at a landscape level. Verification and reporting costs are capped at roughly five percent of each park’s management budget, keeping most funding directed at conservation itself. The Rob Walton Foundation’s executive director described VNUs as a way to direct capital toward measurable, verifiable conservation results. He framed the approach as attractive for philanthropy today, while also testing whether it could eventually support other financing tools. Conservation funding gaps across Africa have long hindered efforts to protect large, ecologically important landscapes. Traditional grants often fund activities such as ranger patrols or fencing without directly tying payment to whether wildlife populations or habitat conditions actually improve. Results-based conservation finance in Africa aims to close that gap by making payments conditional on outcomes verified by an independent party. Results-based conservation finance in Africa addresses a long-standing funding gap by making payment conditional on independently verified improvements in wildlife populations and habitat conditions, rather than simply funding ranger patrols or fencing regardless of whether outcomes improve. Photo by Francesco Ungaro on Pexels. Beyond grants, African Parks says the VNU framework could eventually support bonds, credits, and other nature-linked financial instruments. The goal is a standardized metric that investors and donors can trust across very different ecosystems and countries. Conservation finance has often lacked this consistency, with funding mechanisms and reporting standards varying widely by project. African Parks currently manages 24 parks across 13 African countries, which hold an estimated 12 billion tonnes of stored carbon dioxide equivalent. That scale gives the organization a large testing ground for results-based conservation finance in Africa, where a single standardized metric could eventually apply across dozens of ecosystems at once. According to African Parks, VNUs are designed to support a range of financing mechanisms, including pay-for-performance grants, donations, bonds, and credits. The organization’s next steps include reissuing units, expanding the model to more parks, and attracting a wider mix of funders. Whether this approach spreads beyond African Parks will depend on how reliably verification holds up as the model scales, and whether other funders are willing to adopt a similar standard. For now, the Rob Walton Foundation’s commitment offers one of the clearest real-world tests yet of whether results-based conservation finance in Africa can shift funding away from promises and toward outcomes that donors can actually confirm. The post Results-Based Conservation Finance in Africa Gets a $4.6 Million Boost appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Suzanne Peck , a lecturer of art at the Rochester Institute of Technology, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive, and demanding. When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel, and to find some focus within and among the kinetic. The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability. Glass as a Material At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass . This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash, and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius). In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass . You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave. Picofluidicist/Wikimedia Commons Pyrex cookware is made out of a specially formulated, heat-resistant type of glass called borosilicate. Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid , meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point . Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range. Gathering Glass Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working. We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed. AP Photo/Keith Srakocic Glass artists heat up their glass in a furnace so that it’s molten and easy to mold. When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone — probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid. To make anything — a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb, or a pumpkin — you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions. Elizabeth Lamark/RIT An artist works in the Glass Hot Shop at RIT. When glass is in its molten state, the artist can shape it and blow into it. You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability , allowing you to continue working it without breaking it. A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times. Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone. So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object — utilitarian, domestic, and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete. Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin. Working With Physics I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench, and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years. AP Photo/Gerry Broome Glass artists use a variety of tools to shape their work. I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly. If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer : a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C). This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours. As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble — the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on. The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication, and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky. Κανένας κολυμβητής δεν το άφησε εκεί. Όπως τα περισσότερα από αυτά που συλλέγονται στις πιο δυσπρόσιτες ακτές της Ελλάδας, οδήγησε i…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM At some point in the past three decades, a beer can printed with a Spanish-language ad for a 1990s World Cup washed up on Patroklos, a small islet in the Saronic Gulf about 65 nautical miles (75 miles) from Athens. No swimmer left it there. Like most of what collects on Greece’s harder-to-reach shores, it rode in on the currents, and it stayed until a crew working on a Greek coastline cleanup picked it up, sorted it, and wrote it down. That last step, the writing down, is what makes this project more interesting than a beach sweep. Every bottle, net, and wrapper the crew logs becomes a clue about where the Mediterranean’s waste starts its trip. A Greek coastline cleanup run from the sea The Typhoon and its 20-person crew Greece has the longest coastline of any Mediterranean country, and much of it has no road leading to it. Since July 2019, the Typhoon Project has reached those stretches by water, using a 72-meter (236-foot) ship as its base. Each day, a crew of 20 heads ashore in five inflatable boats and gathers, sorts, and records between 500 and 1,000 kilograms (roughly 1,100 to 2,200 pounds) of waste, which then goes to the appropriate facilities for recycling. The project belongs to the Public Benefit Foundation Athanassios C. Laskaridis , a Greek foundation whose work centers on protecting the environment and the sea in particular. By February 2023, the crew had completed its first full circuit of the islands and most of the mainland coast. Seven years, 1,140 tonnes Across more than 10,000 cleanup operations, the Typhoon has removed 1,140 tonnes (about 1,257 US tons) of trash. Peggy Xirotagarou, the foundation’s executive director, has learned that the number means more to people as an image than as a weight. “To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers,” she said. Marine litter as a research record Counting every item on every beach The cleanup is half the job. The other half happens after the bags are on board, when the crew records what was found, item by item and beach by beach. Thanasis Besios, who manages the Typhoon Project, considers that record as valuable as the cleared sand. “One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day,” he told Euronews. Researchers are putting that record to use. The project works with the Laboratory of Marine Geology and Physical Oceanography at the University of Patras to study waste on the seabed of the Saronic and Thermaic Gulfs, and with the Marine Remote Sensing Research Group at the University of the Aegean, which uses remote sensing technology to locate and map plastics. Tracing coastal pollution back inland The Cyclone program Seven years of sorting led the foundation to an uncomfortable conclusion about its own beaches. Plenty of what lands on the coast was never thrown into the sea in the first place, and illegal, unmanaged landfills are still running in many parts of Greece. “By observing the waste we were finding on the shores, we realised that a large proportion came from inland,” Xirotagarou said. The foundation’s response, launched in 2024, is a land-based counterpart called Cyclone . “It involves large-scale clean-ups in lakes, rivers and archaeological sites. We have created three large teams in different parts of Greece, where every day we collect more than 1,000 kilos of waste,” she said. Schools on every stop Wherever the Typhoon drops anchor, the team also visits local schools, then brings students out to the shoreline. Xirotagarou sees the classroom work as the long game behind the whole operation. “Because that is the ultimate goal. For them to become responsible citizens and for this reckless use of single-use plastics to stop,” she said. A project that began by picking up after the sea has ended up asking where the trash started. A crew can clear an islet in an afternoon, but slowing what reaches it depends on the steadier work the foundation has added since 2024, from the river and lake crews to the classroom visits. The Greek coastline cleanup will keep finding cans like the one on Patroklos, though its logbook now gives Greece a much clearer sense of which ones drifted in from abroad and which started a few miles inland. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Very few Americans have ever eaten foie gras. It’s a niche luxury, served mostly in high-end restaurants, and yet on November 3 it produced some of the most lopsided results of the night in two American cities. In Washington, DC, 73 percent of voters backed a ban on selling the force-fed duck liver, and in Denver, 66 percent did. They weren’t alone. Across this year’s midterms , animal welfare ballot measures had a strong showing, and the pattern in what passed and what didn’t says something about how voters approach animals when the question in front of them is narrow and specific. Foie gras bans win by wide margins How foie gras is produced Foie gras comes from ducks that are force-fed through a metal pipe about 60 times in the final weeks before slaughter, until their livers swell to six to 10 times their natural size. Producers and many fine-dining chefs maintain that the practice is harmless, or at least no worse than other factory farming methods, while veterinary research has concluded it can be quite painful for the birds. DC and Denver join a growing list “Tonight DC decided that force-feeding a bird has no place here,” said Cady Witt of Pro-Animal DC, the group that put the measure on the ballot. The District’s ban on sales takes effect in July 2027 . California, New York City, Pittsburgh, and Portland, Oregon, already restrict foie gras sales, though the earlier city bans came from officials rather than voters, according to Ballotpedia . Outside the U.S., more than 20 European countries prohibit foie gras production; Brazil banned both its sale and production this year, and India has barred imports since 2014. Producers and chefs plan to fight back The votes may not be the last word. A representative from Hudson Valley Farms, the country’s largest foie gras producer, told Axios the company is considering legal challenges. In DC, Bart Hutchins, chef and owner of the restaurant Butterworth’s, wrote in a Washington Post op-ed that he was “incredibly disappointed” the measure reached the ballot, The Hill reported , and he has since hosted four-course foie gras dinners to raise money for a possible lawsuit. Colorado rejects a constitutional hunting amendment What Amendment 83 asked voters Colorado’s Amendment 83 would have written “the right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods” into the state constitution and named hunting and fishing as the preferred way to manage wildlife populations. About 55 percent of voters opposed it, according to unofficial results . Supporters argued that hunting and fishing rights shouldn’t depend on statutes or on whoever sits on the state wildlife commission, and 24 states already have some version of the protection in their constitutions. The amendment also exempted nongame and endangered species. Why “traditional methods” mattered Hunting and fishing are already protected by Colorado statute, so critics focused on the phrase “traditional methods.” “Read plainly, traditional methods could be interpreted to include practices like poisoning, leg hold traps, gill nets, or baiting and hounding,” Rebecca Niemiec, co-director of Colorado State University’s Animal-Human Policy Center and a Colorado Parks and Wildlife commissioner, told Vox in October. Colorado currently bans those practices. Vox reporter Neel Dhanesha described the stakes for animals that were never the intended target: “Steel-jawed traps and poisons don’t discriminate between, say, a deer, a wolf , and a lynx.” Opponents also worried that naming hunting the preferred management tool could sideline alternatives such as wildlife birth control and relocation. Where voters drew the line on animal welfare Conservation funding passes in several states Wildlife habitat did well this year too. Massachusetts voters approved a measure to fund nature conservation, and voters in Brevard County, Florida, renewed a tax that pays for manatee and dolphin habitat restoration. Conservation measures in Arkansas and Rhode Island also passed. Broader bans have a harder time Not every animal measure finds a majority. In 2024, Denver voters turned down a ban on fur sales, which drew 42.4 percent support, and a ban on slaughterhouses within city limits, which drew 36.3 percent, according to Ballotpedia. Set beside this year’s foie gras results, the two votes suggest that measures targeting one specific practice tend to fare better than ones that would reshape a whole industry. Farm animal laws and the candidates who opposed them Several candidate races also touched on animal welfare policy. In 2016, Massachusetts voters banned the sale of eggs and pork from hens and pregnant pigs kept in small cages, and California voters passed a nearly identical law two years later. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas and Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa, both Republicans, have sponsored bills to override those state laws, most recently the Save Our Bacon Act, and both lost their races this year. In Colorado’s Eighth Congressional District, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a state lawmaker and former Earthjustice attorney who sued meat companies over pollution, defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Gabe Evans. In Iowa, Chris Jones, a water quality expert who campaigned on cleaning up livestock and farm pollution, narrowly lost his bid for agriculture secretary. Neither major party has made animal welfare a central campaign issue, but the results will shape how these debates play out in Congress and statehouses over the next two years. For the campaigners in DC, the win came down to thousands of individual signatures and votes, a slow, ground-level way of changing what a city allows on its menus. Witt closed her statement on election night by thanking the people who did that work: “Thank you to everyone who signed the petition and voted to make DC a kinder place for animals.” Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: The bots roll along blood vessels to stir up stagnant blood and push drugs toward clots. Drugs that break up blood clots are vital for treating strokes, heart attacks, and clogged blood vessels in the lungs, but sometimes blockages are so large that medication struggles to get through. Now, researchers are building tiny magnetic robots to help medicines reach their targets. Severe blockages in blood vessels pose a tricky problem. The bloodstream is the only way to deliver clot-busting drugs, but if a clot stops the flow, there is no other way to carry them there. A team at ETH Zurich in Switzerland has a workaround. Magnetically driven microbots that roll along vessel walls can stir up stagnant blood so the drug gets pushed towards the clot. In lab tests, the approach dissolved clots six times faster than with the drug alone, and in experiments on pigs, it restored blood flow to an area twice as large after 30 minutes. “To our knowledge, we are the first to show in a clinically relevant large-animal model that the use of microrobots in this way does indeed enhance thrombolysis [the process of dissolving blood clots],” Schürle said in a press release . The bots are a far cry from your traditional robot. Just eight micrometers long, each is shaped like a grain of rice and made of a sugar-based polymer laced with magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles. During fabrication, the researchers expose the devices to a rotating magnetic field that pushes the nanoparticles into a straight line, essentially creating a bar magnet running the length of each bot. When a magnetic control system outside the body applies a rotating field, the internal magnet spins and causes each bot to tumble head over tail. The bots themselves don’t carry drugs. Rather, they’re released near a blockage along with clot-busting medicine. As the bots roll along the vessel walls towards the restriction, they create currents that carry the drug into the clot. To test the approach, the team built an artificial network of vessel-like channels and plugged it with clots made of pig blood. They compared what happened when they added the clot-dissolving drug alone to what happened when they added the drug and the bots together. Adding the bots cleared the clots six times faster than when they tried just the drug. To see if the strategy would work in real biological systems, the team blocked arteries in live pigs and treated them with just drugs and drugs plus microbots. After 30 minutes, the area with restored blood flow was twice as large in animals that received the bots. The work adds to a growing body of research into clot-busting magnetic microrobots. Last year, a separate ETH Zurich team led by Bradley Nelson published a paper in Science describing a dissolvable gel capsule that could be steered through blood vessels and release a clot-dissolving drug when heated by a high-frequency magnetic field. Others have taken a more mechanical approach. Researchers at the University of Twente and Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands used 3D-printed, screw-shaped robots containing tiny magnets to drill into clots, removing enough material from a blocked artery taken from a sheep to get blood flowing again. While the ETH team have filed a patent application for their bots, it’s still early. The paper describing the results has yet to clear peer review, and human trials are a long way off. Nonetheless, the results are another indication that microrobots could one day become a valuable new tool in a doctor’s arsenal. The post Tiny Magnetic Robots Help Dissolve Blood Clots Six Times Faster Than With Drugs Alone appeared first on SingularityHub .

Mushroom coffins and green burial options give families a new way to care for the planet. Loop Biotech , a company in Delft, the Netherlands, grows these products from living mushroom roots. The company says traditional funerals can harm the environment. It points to cutting old trees, releasing carbon dioxide, and adding toxic chemicals to soil. Loop Biotech wants to offer a gentler choice. Interest in greener funerals is growing. A 2023 report from the National Funeral Directors Association found that 60% of consumers would explore green funeral options. That is about six in every ten people, so mushroom coffins and green burials meet a real demand. The idea began at Delft University of Technology. Founders Bob and Lonneke Hendrikx were graduating there when they asked a simple question: Could a final act help the earth instead of harming it? They found an answer in mycelium, the root network of mushrooms. It grows underground and breaks down dead plant matter. As it does, it releases nutrients that feed new life. Mycelium is known as one of nature’s biggest recyclers. Researchers have only recently given it close attention. For years, many of them focused on plants and animals above ground. Loop Biotech grows its products from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers. Upcycled means the fibers are reused instead of thrown away. Hemp is a tough plant often used for rope and cloth. The growing process takes just seven days. Trees used for traditional coffins can take many decades to grow. That difference shows how quickly this material can be made. Once the coffin is buried, it begins to break down. The company says it biodegrades in about 45 days. Mushroom coffins and green burial materials like these return to the soil faster than most wood and metal. The coffin is also strong. Hendrikx says it can carry about 440 pounds (200 kilograms). He adds that people are often surprised by how soft and sturdy it feels. The company invented the world’s first mushroom coffin, called the Loop Living Cocoon. It also makes the Loop EarthRise and the Loop ForestBed. The company describes its products as patented and award-winning. Mushroom coffins and green burial options now include the Loop EarthRise, the world’s first urn made from mushrooms, grown in seven days from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers to nourish the earth and grow a tree in your memory. Photo courtesy of Loop Biotech . Each product is 100% natural and biodegradable. Biodegradable means it breaks down naturally over time. The company also says its products enrich the soil. Soil-enriching is a bold claim, so families should look at the details. Asking a funeral provider about materials, local rules, and cemetery policies is a smart first step. Green burial is a broader movement. It generally avoids embalming chemicals and uses naturally biodegradable materials. Mushroom coffins and green burial fit together because both aim to leave the ground healthier. Why does this matter to families? Many people want a funeral that matches how they lived. For someone who loved gardens or forests, a soil-enriching option may feel personal. Loop Biotech describes its approach as working with nature rather than against it. The founders chose living organisms over dead materials. That idea shapes every product the company grows. The founders describe their mission as turning endings into new beginnings. This view invites people to think about death differently. It treats a funeral as part of a natural cycle. The company grows its products at a facility in Delft, close to where the founders studied. Local mushrooms keep the process tied to the region. That choice also supports the company’s goal of a positive footprint. A footprint is the mark people leave on the environment. The company wants that mark to be positive. It aims to return nutrients to the soil. Demand is spreading beyond Europe. Hendrikx estimates it has sold more than 2,000 coffins in Europe and has started selling in North America. Mushroom coffins and green burial alternatives are now reaching families on both continents. The company shares a brand video. It tells the story behind the products and the people who make them. For more detail, people can watch a TEDx talk by Bob Hendrikx. TEDx is an independently organized event that follows the TED talk format. He explains how mycelium works, how the products grow in seven days, and his vision of a regenerative world that restores natural systems. Mushroom coffins are one of several ideas for gentler goodbyes. Families are also finding new ways to honor loved ones while protecting the planet. Choosing a funeral involves many feelings and practical questions. Families who want an earth-friendly path now have more to consider. Mushroom coffins and green burial may help more people leave a positive mark. The post Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Ο ιδιοκτήτης Σον Γουάιτ ολοκληρώνει την περικοπή για έναν μεσήλικα μαύρο ενώ ένας άλλος πελάτης περιμένει εκεί κοντά. items.descriptionOriginal: I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says. The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives. Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how comfortable they were discussing intimate concerns — and how closely they listened to their barber. “It’s been said to me many times that many Black men trust their barber more than they trust their doctor,” he says. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] CLIP sought to build on that familiarity as a way to reach people with undiagnosed hypertension. The condition is both common and easy to miss. About six in 10 non-Hispanic Black men in the United States have hypertension, according to federal data. Yet high blood pressure often produces no symptoms. Among men ages 18 to 39 who have hypertension, the federal data found, fewer than one in four know they have it . Routine access to health care can make early detection more likely, but access is only part of the problem. A 2019 study linked medical mistrust and perceived racism in health care with delayed checkups and blood-pressure screening among Black men. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” says Sean White. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Led by NYU Langone in partnership with Community Health Action of Staten Island (CHASI), CLIP brought blood-pressure screening and health support into 22 Black-owned barbershops from Staten Island zip codes with high hypertension prevalence . Against Da Grain was one of them. W hite’s appointments that Tuesday often stretched beyond 30 minutes. “The barber chair is perfectly set up for measuring blood pressure,” Ravenell says. Some patients experience what’s known as “white coat syndrome,” meaning the stress of a clinical setting causes their blood pressure to rise temporarily. By contrast, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened, so with proper technique, a reading taken at the barber shop may better reflect their usual levels. The challenge, Ravenell adds, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Unlike in a clinical setting, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened. Credit: Tolu Olasoji During CLIP, local Black male community health workers measured patrons’ blood pressure, counseled them, and connected them with medical and social services. Barbers encouraged customers to participate, but screenings were offered without pressure. “I allowed the men to decide whether they wanted to engage with me,” says a community health worker. Importantly, the community health workers were often themselves customers at the participating barbershops and knew the barbers and customers. Ravenell says that familiarity meant “their presence is not an intrusion, as it might be for someone with a white coat.” Across the program, 636 men were screened. Four hundred sixty-one were found to have elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension, 430 of whom enrolled in the study. Participants were 38 years old on average; only 24 percent reported having a primary care provider, and about half had health insurance. The study followed up with enrolled men at six-month intervals through 18 months, even after recruitment at individual shops had ended. At 18 months, community health workers obtained a repeat blood-pressure reading from 96 percent of participants. That level of follow-up, Ravenell says, is unusual and difficult to achieve in a long-running study. Dr. Chidinma Ibe, a community health workers researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Equity, calls the figures “extremely, extremely impressive,” adding that they reinforce the value of meeting people where they are. D espite these successes, however, CLIP did not produce the primary result researchers had hoped for . At 12 months, participants’ systolic blood pressure had changed little. Fewer men met the study’s definition of incident stage two hypertension at 12 months, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at 18 months. Dr. Ibe says that given that the intervention was among men with elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension rather than severely uncontrolled disease, the limited movement in its main blood-pressure outcome was “not terribly surprising.” The challenge for CLIP, notes Dr. Joseph Ravenell, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji For Derek Griffith, a University of Pennsylvania professor who studies Black men’s health, success in simply reaching men is separate from controlling their blood pressure. He says the major determinants of blood-pressure control remain in what men experience outside both barbershops and clinical care. Dr. Idris Robinson, research project manager for Penn’s Program for Research on Men’s Health, likewise cautions against treating the barbershop itself as the intervention. “The blood pressure outcomes weren’t rooted in some magical equation where barbers plus Black men equals guaranteed improvements in Black men’s health,” he says. Sustained engagement, he argues, also depends on collaboration among academic and community partners, barbers’ relationships with clients, and a wider support network. “That infrastructure is critical.” That becomes crucial after an elevated reading. When this occurred with CLIP participants, community health workers explained what the number could mean and encouraged medical follow-up. When it came to a referral, notes Joseph Ebron, CHASI’s director of health equity, “We would let them know what we offer, but it was up to them to take it.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji Even when people wanted help, navigating existing services could complicate the handoff. Workers sometimes met people who thought they lacked coverage, only to discover they were already enrolled elsewhere but were not getting the help they needed. And because they were already attached to another provider or organization, CHASI could not always simply move them into a different service. “We can’t just, like, snatch them,” says Ebron. Ibe points to a structural problem behind that handoff: the fragmented American health care system. Insurance issues, the absence of an established primary care relationship, and weak connections between community organizations and clinical teams can all interrupt the route to care. “If the [community health worker] isn’t employed by that clinic, there’s only so much they can do,” she says. Sustaining even the community side required labor. Active recruitment through Against Da Grain lasted about two months. “We did it for some time without receiving any type of payments,” says White, adding that the program brought “a lot of extra work.” CHASI adapted around the business in real-time: For instance, Ebron says to work around Against Da Grain’s preferences, they screened outside, where workers could pull up a small mobile health unit and barbers could direct interested customers to it. Workers learned to take up less space, getting rid of tables and flyers in favor of a simpler setup: a blood-pressure monitor and materials carried in a bag. Though CLIP is now over, there are larger screening events every two to three months and health workers can return to shops when requested. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Ravenell sees funding — and therefore sustainability — as the broader limitation. When CLIP ended in September 2025, he says Staten Island screening partners continued some services “essentially pro bono” during a funding gap. His team has since received two new NIH grants to build on CLIP’s infrastructure and train community health workers to screen in barbershops for diabetes and diabetic eye disease. For now, CLIP itself is over, though Ebron says CHASI conducts larger screening events every two to three months and can return to shops when requested. Whether the model can travel is another question. Ravenell says Staten Island had an advantage before CLIP began: CHASI had already spent more than 30 years working in the borough through community health workers. “Replicated, yes, easily, no,” Ebron says, because success depends on what already exists locally. CLIP reinforced White’s sense of responsibility to the community he has served for more than 35 years, while sharpening his awareness of the health concerns moving through it. “It helped me realize how many people have elevated levels,” he says. Join Cancel anytime Around noon at Against Da Grain, White’s final appointment brings in a young couple and their son, there for the boy’s first haircut. His mother livestreams the occasion to relatives. When the boy climbs down, his father takes his place in the chair. One generation giving way to another, if only for a haircut. Όταν η Lilly Pettus έφερε μια καρέκλα τραπεζαρίας -- μετακόμισε σε έξι πολιτείες για τριάντα χρόνια, κρατώντας στο ξύλο της το βάρος του οικογενειακού γέλιου και της σκληρής συνέλευσης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Across church basements and community halls, Americans are gathering not just to fix broken lamps and cracked chairs, but to push back against an economy that profits from loneliness and waste. When Lilly Pettus brought a dining room chair -- moved across six states over thirty years, holding in its wood the weight of family laughter and hard conversations -- to a repair caf in Decatur, Georgia, she left with something more than a mended joint: strangers' hands had pressed her family's history back together. "When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it's very lonely," says Martine Postma, who founded Repair Caf International in 2010, and the repair caf s she helped seed around the world are a quiet argument against that loneliness. In neighborhoods where the need is economic as much as environmental, and in ones where it is sentimental, the impulse turns out to be the same: a refusal to let things, and the connections they carry, be so easily discarded. What these gatherings reveal, almost incidentally, is that the skills of care have never really disappeared; they've just been waiting for a place to gather.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries Reading Time: 3 minutes Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide have expanded from a single German packaging rule in 1991 into a global compliance landscape spanning more than 70 countries today. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide shift the financial and physical burden of waste management from governments and taxpayers to the companies that manufacture and sell products. Under these laws, producers must collect, recycle, and properly dispose of the packaging and products they put on the market, fundamentally changing the economics of how goods are designed and sold. The concept traces back to Germany’s Packaging Ordinance of 1991, the world’s first EPR regulation. At the time, packaging waste accounted for roughly half of landfill volume and a third of total waste in Germany, pushing national landfill capacity toward its limits and forcing policymakers to act. More than three decades later, extended producer responsibility laws worldwide have evolved from that single national response into one of the most significant regulatory trends reshaping global manufacturing and retail. Europe remains the most mature region for these frameworks, with approximately 40 to 45 countries now operating established EPR schemes. The European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which entered into force in February 2025 and applies fully from August 2026, replaced the previous directive with uniform, directly applicable requirements across all member states. The regulation requires packaging to meet EU recyclability performance criteria, sets recycled-content targets for plastic packaging starting in 2030, and restricts PFAS in food-contact packaging starting in August 2026. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide increasingly extend beyond packaging alone. France’s framework, codified in its Environmental Code in 1992, now covers packaging, paper, textiles, electrical and electronic equipment, and batteries, with industrial and commercial packaging added to the scope in January 2025. This expansion reflects a broader pattern: once EPR infrastructure exists for one product category, governments frequently extend similar accountability to additional waste streams. In Asia, Japan’s Container and Packaging Recycling Law dates to 1997, obligating producers to fund recycling for designated packaging materials, while recent circular economy obligations have supplemented rather than replaced that core framework. South Korea operates what is widely considered one of the strictest EPR systems globally under its Resource Circulation Act, requiring companies to reduce packaging weight, improve recyclability, and submit to public disclosure of violators as a reputational enforcement mechanism alongside heavy fines. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide increasingly rely on eco-modulated fees that reward recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed packaging, creating market pressure for companies across Europe, Asia, and the Americas to redesign products proactively rather than simply absorbing compliance costs. Photo by Mikhail Nilov on Pexels. China’s approach folds extended producer responsibility obligations into its broader Law on Prevention and Control of Environmental Pollution by Solid Waste, expanding registration and recycling reporting requirements for both electronics and packaging sectors. India’s Plastic Waste Rules, first introduced in 2016 and amended in 2022, require producers, importers, and brand owners to register and take direct responsibility for collecting, recycling, or disposing of plastic packaging waste they introduce into the market. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide show particularly rapid momentum across the Americas. In Canada, most provinces are fully transitioning to EPR models for packaging and printed paper, requiring registration with provincial programs, annual reporting by material type and weight, and payment of eco-modulated fees that vary by packaging performance and recyclability. Brazil’s National Policy on Solid Waste requires manufacturers, importers, distributors, and sellers to implement reverse-logistics systems that ensure packaging is reused or recycled rather than discarded. Chile’s Law 20.920 similarly requires producers of priority products to establish their own collection, recovery, and recycling schemes to meet government-set targets. In the United States, more than half a dozen states have already implemented EPR legislation, with additional states expected to follow as the model gains bipartisan traction. This state-by-state approach creates a patchwork of overlapping requirements that producers selling nationally must navigate simultaneously. Beyond mandatory frameworks, some nations have pursued voluntary or co-regulatory pathways as stepping stones toward fuller accountability. Australia’s National Packaging Targets, administered by the Australian Packaging Covenant Organization, aim for 100% of packaging to be recyclable, reusable, or compostable and operate through industry-led stewardship rather than direct government mandate. New Zealand has introduced voluntary EPR initiatives for packaging, with mandatory requirements expected as the voluntary phase matures. A common thread across extended producer responsibility laws worldwide is eco-modulated fee structures, financial penalties or incentives tied directly to how recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed a product’s packaging is. This design creates market pressure encouraging companies to redesign packaging proactively rather than simply paying compliance costs passively, since better-designed packaging typically carries lower fees under most EPR schemes. For companies operating or distributing products internationally, this patchwork of national and regional requirements creates genuine compliance complexity. Registration requirements, reporting formats, fee structures, and penalty regimes vary significantly by country, even as the underlying principle that producers bear responsibility for their products’ end-of-life impact remains consistent across jurisdictions. As extended producer responsibility laws worldwide continue expanding into new product categories and new countries, the regulatory trajectory points firmly in one direction: toward holding manufacturers accountable not just for what they sell, but for what eventually becomes of it, transforming waste management from a public cost into a cost of doing business built directly into product design and corporate strategy. The post Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Η συσκευή καρπού του Tourette, που ονομάζεται Neupulse, προέκυψε από έρευνα στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Νότιγχαμ και τρία χρόνια μετά, οι άνθρωποι που τη χρησιμοποιούν περιγράφουν την επίδρασή της πολύ πιο ισχυρά.…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse , came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe its effect in far stronger terms than a one-in-four reduction would suggest. How a Tourette’s wrist device targets tics Rhythmic pulses to the median nerve Neupulse sends rhythmic electrical pulses into the median nerve, which runs through the wrist and into the hand. Trials have shown that this stimulation changes activity in the brain regions responsible for movement control, and that the rhythm of the pulses can lower both the frequency and the intensity of tics. The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company, Neurotherapeutics Ltd, which secured £1 million (about $1.3 million) in additional funding to bring it to market. Stephen Jackson, the Nottingham professor who has led the research, described the response from users as “a dream come true.” Some of the feedback he has received is very concrete. “We’ve had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking,” he said. Others told the team they could move through an airport and board a flight without tics. Tourette’s syndrome in the UK Tourette’s syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition, usually beginning in childhood, that causes involuntary sounds and movements known as tics. More than 300,000 people in the UK have it, according to the charity Tourettes Action , and there is no cure. The condition reached a wider audience in 2023 when singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette’s, tried the device before a concert in Nottingham, and again through the film I Swear , a drama based on the life of Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson. Three users, three measurable changes Katie, 15: years of constant vocal tics Katie, from Hertfordshire, started having tics at age seven. Her snorting tic ran almost nonstop, to the point of leaving her with a sore throat that kept her in bed for two weeks, and it disrupted her sleep, her eating, and her school attendance. “It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, ‘why are you doing that?'” she said. Her mom, Julia, called it “heartbreaking” to watch. “You feel helpless. You feel you don’t know where to turn really,” she said. After reading about the Nottingham research, Julia brought Katie to try the device in December, before it went on sale. The effect was immediate, Katie said, and she became “really calm.” “It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life,” she said. On the drive back to Hertfordshire, she “just cried the whole way home.” Ollie, 15: a different diagnosis, a similar response Ollie’s case extends the picture, because he does not have Tourette’s. Nearly two years ago he cracked his neck, and about 48 hours later the movement had become involuntary and constant. “It was incredibly sudden,” he said. He was later diagnosed with functional neurological disorder (FND), a condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals. His father, Alex, said sleeping, eating and drinking all became “incredibly difficult.” Ollie stayed inside for about a month at one stage and missed six to seven months of school ahead of his GCSEs, the exams British students sit around age 16. He came close to telling his parents not to bother with the device. A few months ago, when he switched it on for the first time, he phoned home. “You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped,” Alex said. Ollie put it this way: “It’s like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it’s like getting part of your life back.” Mylo, 17: from trial participant to owner Mylo, from Buckinghamshire, was 13 when he joined the 2023 trial. He recently received his own device as a gift and said the urge to suppress his facial tics went away “instantaneously.” “As soon as it comes on, I can feel it,” he said. “I feel different… I feel new almost, which is strange.” Why Neupulse is not yet an NHS treatment Wellness product versus medical device The device comes in two versions. Neupulse-C is sold as a consumer wellness product, and the university says “thousands” have been purchased. Neupulse-M is the version intended for marketing as a medical treatment for tics and Tourette’s syndrome, and it is still working through regulatory approval. That distinction determines whether the National Health Service can offer it. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has identified the technology as “promising” but asked for more evidence of long-term benefit. In 2025, it said its committee would meet again to assess the device’s clinical and cost-effectiveness. “They were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval,” Jackson said. “That’s something we’re working towards.” He hopes to see the Tourette’s wrist device available through the NHS “in the next year or so.” Early reports from the Tourette’s community Emma McNally, CEO of Tourettes Action , said the users she has spoken with have given the device “nothing but praise.” “Some people have said it’s helped them to go to places that they’ve not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library,” she said. Others told her it helped them come out of a tic attack and feel more relaxed. Wrist stimulation beyond Tourette’s syndrome The Nottingham team is now testing the same approach on other conditions. Early trials have examined whether the pulses can reduce tremors in people with Parkinson’s , and Jackson said the university plans a UK-wide clinical trial covering anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The next milestone is regulatory, since medical approval for Neupulse-M would open the door to NICE guidance and NHS prescriptions, and the trials that follow will show whether a signal sent through the wrist can shape movement and mood in conditions well beyond tics. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You know that feeling when it’s two in the afternoon, and you can’t quite account for where the morning went? Not because you weren’t doing things, but because the busyness didn’t add up to anything you can point to. It’s demoralizing in a specific way, and it has surprisingly little to do with how early your alarm went off. Time management experts Melinda Rathkopf, M.D., M.B.A. , and Julie Morgenstern , the author of multiple bestselling books on productivity, say most of what shapes your morning was set in motion the night before, and the solution is usually far simpler than the elaborate routines you’ve seen floating around online. Start the night before Where do both experts begin? The evening before. When you make decisions about tomorrow before you go to sleep, you take some of the friction out of the morning itself. “Preplanning the day ahead and making decisions ahead of time makes the rest of your day potentially calmer and less stressful,” says Rathkopf. “Set yourself up by knowing what’s coming.” Transition time is one of the things that tends to get left out when people plan their days. It’s easy to schedule back-to-back tasks and forget that moving between them really does take time. Build that in the night before and the morning feels a lot less like you’re already behind before you’ve started. This extends to sleep, too. Rathkopf recommends starting with how much sleep you genuinely need to feel refreshed, then working backward from your wake time to set a consistent bedtime. “ Sleep is so vital to daily functioning and brain health,” she says. Most people schedule everything else first and try to fit sleep in around it. She suggests reversing that. Put the phone away before bed and after waking up If there’s one habit both experts come back to, it’s keeping your phone out of your first and last hour of each day. Morgenstern is direct about it. “The number one thing that can boost morning productivity has to do with screen time ,” she says. “We should not be on our devices an hour before bed, and we should not be on our devices for our first hour of the morning.” Checking your phone first thing does more than eat up time. It pulls you into a reactive state before you’ve had a chance to figure out your own priorities for the day. “The phone can be a useful tool, but it’s designed to keep us on there,” Morgenstern says. “Think of it like sugar — you have to really manage your consumption, and take charge. It’s the key to morning productivity, engagement, your relationships, everything.” She recommends replacing that screen time with something restorative: reading, getting outside, or having a conversation with someone. The goal isn’t deprivation; it’s starting the day on your own terms instead of somebody else’s notifications. Keep your routine simple One persistent myth about productive mornings is that they require an elaborate ritual. If you’ve ever felt vaguely inadequate watching someone describe their two-hour routine involving cold plunges , journaling, and a complicated smoothie, you’re not alone. Those routines often backfire. “It can make you stressed out — ‘Oh god, I didn’t meditate long enough!'” Morgenstern says. “Add three to four elements maximum for a morning routine. Otherwise, you’re habituating to something that’s unsustainable.” Find the small handful of things that reliably start your morning feeling calm and grounded, and stick with those. If you’re getting ready alongside young children, Morgenstern suggests completing your own routine before they’re up, then putting some thought into making their mornings smoother too. Laying out clothes or choosing breakfast the night before can take a surprising amount of stress out of a weekday morning. Train your brain with predictability Your brain is a creature of habit in the most useful sense. “Our brains love predictability,” says Rathkopf. “When you have a predictable routine, you’re reducing your stress and cognitive load.” When your morning follows a consistent pattern, you spend less mental energy on logistics and more on the work itself, which sounds obvious until you notice how rarely most mornings feel that way in practice. Morgenstern describes building a regular block for deep thinking as a kind of training for your brain: “If you have a predictable head-down time, your brain gets acclimated to it — it’s 10:30, that’s when we do our deep thinking. I’ve never seen anyone build proactive work with an erratic schedule.” For creative work especially, consistency turns out to matter more than inspiration. Start with the work that matters most A lot of mornings get swallowed by emails, messages, and reactive tasks before you ever reach work that needs your purest attention. “The number one difficulty people have is that the day starts off all reactive, and they can’t get to proactive work,” Morgenstern says. Her suggestion is to start with the most important thing on your list, the one that needs your freshest thinking. Even if everything else gets away from you after that, you’ve done something that mattered. “Even if you only get that one thing done, you’ll feel the greatest sense of relief that you’ve done your job,” she says. If your workplace opens with a morning meeting, Morgenstern recommends blocking off a half hour to an hour right after it for focused work, to address anything that came out of the meeting before settling into your main task. Better yet, see if you can get your whole team to protect the first hour of the day. Build in small moments of recovery Self-care doesn’t need to be a whole thing. What Morgenstern recommends is more modest: short pauses woven throughout the day, especially during your busiest stretches. “Add microbursts of self-care in your day — five to 20-minute activities that recharge you,” she says. A short walk, some music on your commute, ten minutes with a book. Small enough to fit into almost any day, and consistent enough to keep you from burning out by three in the afternoon. “The harder you’re working, the harder you have to recover,” she says. Stopping feels like the last thing you can afford when you’re slammed, but that’s usually when it matters most. Give yourself room to change, and to have off days Both experts caution against treating your morning routine as something fixed. Life changes, seasons change, your circumstances shift, and what works at one stage may not work at another. “You may need to change it based on other obligations, at different stages of your life, or even in different seasons,” says Rathkopf. And when a morning doesn’t come together the way you hoped, she has one more piece of advice: don’t be hard on yourself about it. “Everybody’s different, and what you’re seeing in posts is someone else’s best versions and best days,” Rathkopf says. “They have those not-so-perfect days, too.” A morning routine isn’t something you get right once. It’s something you keep adjusting until it fits. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.description: Οι προτάσεις επιλέγονται ανεξάρτητα από την ομάδα μας, αλλά ενδέχεται να προκύψει προμήθεια στο Nice News, κάτι που βοηθά να διατηρείται το περιεχόμενό μας ελεύθερο.
